extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars of political theory and law
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the normative principles and rules Hobbes states about forms of government, rights of succession, kinds of dominion (paternal/despotic), and the liberty of subjects. Covers how succession is determined, how different sovereignties operate, and what liberty consists in under civil covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three forms of Soveraigntie: Monarchie (one man), Democracie (the general assembly), and Aristocracie (an assembly of certain persons distinguished from the rest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixed or modified governments (elective kingdoms, limited kings, provinces governed by magistrates of another commonwealth) are to be understood in terms of which body actually holds supreme power; elective or limited kings are not sovereign in propriety but ministers of the sovereign. Examples and distinctions are given (e.g., Rome and subject provinces) to show how apparent mixed forms are classified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tutor/Tuition for infant monarchs must preserve authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a monarch appoints a tutor or fails to appoint a tutor for an infant successor, custody (tuition) should be in whoever has most interest in preserving the infant's authority and least to gain by his death or diminution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the precedent monarch appoints a tutor, misgovernment under a child is to be attributed to the ambition or injustice of subjects, not to monarchy. If no provision is taken, the natural rule is to place the child with the person who best preserves the authority (to avoid 'trechery' by those who would profit from the child's destruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies can lack individual liberty to dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: In great commonwealths where sovereignty is in a great assembly, the assembly lacks the liberty to dissent from the counsel of the major part, making its condition analogous to a child who must follow the advice of his tutor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because assemblies are similarly constrained, in great dangers they may need temporary protectors or dictators (Custodes Libertatis) who exercise full authority for a time; such protectors have often been deprived of power more frequently than infant kings have been by their tutors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of succession in monarchy rests with the present sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: By the institution of monarchy the disposing of the successor is left to the judgment and will of the present possessor; if no power to appoint exists, the commonwealth may dissolve or an assembly that has the power must be known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an elected king can appoint his successor he is effectively hereditary; if there is no one known who can give sovereignty after his death, then he is obliged by the law of nature to establish a successor to prevent dissolution into war. The death of a sovereign leaves the multitude without a representative and thus incapable of orderly election unless prior authority exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession passes by express words or testament
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a monarch declares who shall be his heir by viva voce or writing (testament), that person immediately upon the predecessor's death is invested in the right of being monarch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'heire' does not imply children only but whomever the man declares to succeed him; examples include the early Roman emperors naming their heirs expressly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by custom (not controlling a custome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is an established custom that the next of kindred succeeds (or that the next male kindred succeeds), that custom indicates right of succession; failure to controul a custom by express declaration is a natural sign of consent to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale: if the sovereign's will had been otherwise he could have declared it in life; hence existing customary succession stands as his tacit choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by presumption of natural affection
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of testament and custom, it is presumed a monarch wills the monarchy to remain, prefers his own child (male or female) before others, prefers males over females, and prefers nearer blood (siblings) over strangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption rests on natural inclinations (parents favoring children) and the presumed greater fitness of males for dangerous labor; it also orders succession proximities by nearness of blood as reflecting nearness in affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of disposing succession to a foreigner
rubrics_metrics.description: It is lawful for a monarch to dispose of the succession by contract or testament to a king of another nation or a stranger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this can cause inconvenience or oppression if governors are unskilful, the inconvenience proceeds from the governors' faults, not from the act itself; examples (Roman incorporation of elites, proposed union of England and Scotland) show how best to mitigate practical harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of succession follows rights of possession across regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules determining the right of succession mirror the rules for rights of possession: in a democracy the whole assembly cannot fail except if the multitude itself fails; in an aristocracy the assembly (sovereign) elects replacements; in monarchy the present monarch disposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects forms-of-government-specific mechanisms for continuity: democracy's continuity is inherent in the multitude, aristocracy uses collective replacement, monarchy relies on the present possessor's disposal to avoid dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion paternal is founded on consent, contract, or precedent, not mere generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternall dominion (a parent's right over children) is not derived solely from generation but from the child's consent — either express contract, other sufficient signs, education, or precedent subjection; without contract, the dominion is in the mother (who initially nourishes and has custody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: because two parents cannot both be master (one cannot obey two masters), and because in mere nature (no matrimonial law) who nourishes/preserves the child has authority. Historical examples (Amazons) show parental agreements altering dominion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion follows the dominion of residence and parental subjection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If parents (monarchs of separate realms) contract over dominion of their child, right passes by contract; if none, dominion follows the dominion of the place of residence; if one parent is subject to the other, the child's dominion follows that of the parent who is sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the sovereign of each country has dominion over those who reside there; prior subjection of a parent determines child's subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominion extends to descendants and possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: One who has dominion over a person has dominion also over their children and all that belongs to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise dominion would be merely titular without effect; the master holds life and property rights over the person and their issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotic dominion arises only by the vanquished's covenant, not merely by victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominion by conquest (despotical) is acquired when the vanquished, to avoid death or bonds, covenant in express words or sufficient signs to allow the victor use of his life and liberty at the victor's pleasure; mere defeat does not create obligation without the covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: quarter (yielding) defers immediate death but does not guarantee life until the victor permits corporal liberty; the obligation of the vanquished arises from his own promise/submission, not from the victor's act alone. Consequences: the master of a servant may exact goods, labour, children as he sees fit while the covenant holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and consequences of paternall/despotic dominion mirror sovereign rights by institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of both paternall and despotic dominion correspond to the rights of a sovereign by institution: authority over life, property, judicature, appointment of officers, rewards, and punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person who is monarch of nations held by institution and by conquest holds absolute sovereignty in both alike; to treat them differently (demand more from conquered) is ignorance of sovereignty's nature and would justify subjects defending themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign powers enumerated (scope of sovereign authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign (whether by institution or acquisition) cannot have his power transferred without consent, cannot be accused or punished by subjects, and is judge of necessities for peace, doctrines, sole legislator, supreme judge of controversies, controller of war and peace, chooser of magistrates and officers, and determiner of rewards, punishments, honour, and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are given as necessary to prevent perpetual war; the same reasons apply to sovereigns by institution or by conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined as absence of external impediments of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty (freedome) properly signifies absence of external opposition (impediments of motion); a free-man is one who, in things his strength and wit permit, is not hindered from doing what he wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This physical metaphor extends to animate and inanimate things; using 'liberty' for non-motional things is an abuse. Examples: a bound man lacks liberty; water held by banks lacks liberty to spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty of subjects consists in liberty from covenants only where sovereign praetermits
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of subjects pertains to those actions which the sovereign has praetermitted (not regulated) by law — e.g., buying, selling, contracting, choosing abode, diet, trade, and how to educate children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because commonwealth laws cannot regulate every action, in all things not regulated by law subjects retain liberty; but this liberty does not abolish the sovereign's power of life and death, nor absolve subjects from civil obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty is consistent with fear and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions done out of fear or necessity can still be free: a man may throw goods into the sea for fear a ship will sink but still does so willingly; voluntary actions proceed from will yet are causally determined in a chain (necessity), so liberty and necessity are compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: paying a debt out of fear of imprisonment is still an act of a free man in Hobbes' sense; theological remark that God's providence establishes necessity even of voluntary acts without negating human liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial civil bonds (covenants) limit liberty but are upheld by danger
rubrics_metrics.description: Men create artificial chains (civil laws) by mutual covenants attaching obligations to the sovereign and to themselves; these bonds are naturally weak but can be made to hold by the danger of breaking them (i.e., by sovereign enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promises made under fear of death or violence are not covenants when the promised thing is not the promisor's right; nevertheless these artificial bonds form the basis of civil liberty and law within the commonwealth.
